subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: Section 3(7) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 defines a corporate person so as to exclude a financial service provider. Which of the following is therefore outside the scope of the Code?

options.A: An insurance company, being a financial service provider within the meaning of the Code
options.B: A limited liability partnership registered under the Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008
options.C: A company incorporated under a special Act of Parliament and carrying on manufacturing activity
options.D: A body corporate incorporated with limited liability under any law for the time being in force

answer_html:
Answer: (A) An insurance company, being a financial service provider within the meaning of the Code.

Corporate person means a company under Section 2(20) of the Companies Act, 2013, an LLP under the Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008, or any other person incorporated with limited liability under any law in force, but shall not include any financial service provider. The Code therefore does not cover banks, financial institutions, insurance companies, asset reconstruction companies, mutual funds, collective investment schemes or pension funds.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: Under Section 5(12), the insolvency commencement date is the date on which-

options.A: the interim resolution professional causes the public announcement calling for submission of claims
options.B: an application for initiating the corporate insolvency resolution process is admitted by the Adjudicating Authority
options.C: a financial creditor, operational creditor or corporate applicant makes the application to the Adjudicating Authority
options.D: the corporate debtor first commits the default in respect of the debt on which the application is founded

answer_html:
Answer: (B) an application for initiating the corporate insolvency resolution process is admitted by the Adjudicating Authority.

Insolvency commencement date means the date of admission of an application for initiating the corporate insolvency resolution process by the Adjudicating Authority under Section 7, 9 or 10. The date on which the application is made is the initiation date under Section 5(11), which is a different concept. Where no interim resolution professional is appointed in the order of admission, the commencement date is the date on which the interim resolution professional is appointed by the Adjudicating Authority.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: Sunrise Realtors Limited has raised substantial advances from allottees of its housing project. In the corporate insolvency resolution process of the company these allottees will be treated as-

options.A: operational creditors, since the amount is a claim in respect of the provision of goods or services
options.B: secured creditors, since the allotted units stand charged in their favour by operation of law
options.C: unsecured creditors ranking after the Government dues in the order of priority of payment
options.D: financial creditors, since such an amount is deemed to have the commercial effect of a borrowing

answer_html:
Answer: (D) financial creditors, since such an amount is deemed to have the commercial effect of a borrowing.

The Explanation to Section 5(8) provides that any amount raised from an allottee under a real estate project shall be deemed to be an amount having the commercial effect of a borrowing. It is therefore a financial debt, and the allottee is a financial creditor entitled to a place on the committee of creditors. An operational debt under Section 5(21) is a claim in respect of goods or services, employment, or dues payable under any law to a Government or local authority.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: Which of the following is NOT a related party of a corporate debtor within the meaning of Section 5(24)?

options.A: A person who has more than two directors in common with the corporate debtor
options.B: A person controlling fifteen per cent of the voting rights in the corporate debtor under a voting agreement
options.C: A private company in which a manager of the corporate debtor is a director and holds, with his relatives, five per cent of its share capital
options.D: A body corporate which is a holding, subsidiary or associate company of the corporate debtor

answer_html:
Answer: (B) A person controlling fifteen per cent of the voting rights in the corporate debtor under a voting agreement.

Clause (j) of Section 5(24) catches only a person who controls more than twenty per cent of the voting rights in the corporate debtor on account of ownership or a voting agreement, so a holding of fifteen per cent falls outside it. The private company in the second option is caught because the threshold there is a holding of more than two per cent of share capital, and the remaining two options are expressly covered by clauses (i) and (m).

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: The expression insolvency resolution process period in Section 5(14) means the period of-

options.A: 180 days beginning from the initiation date and ending on the one hundred and eightieth day thereafter
options.B: 270 days beginning from the insolvency commencement date, inclusive of every extension granted
options.C: 365 days beginning from the date on which the corporate debtor committed the default in question
options.D: 180 days beginning from the insolvency commencement date and ending on the one hundred and eightieth day

answer_html:
Answer: (D) 180 days beginning from the insolvency commencement date and ending on the one hundred and eightieth day.

Section 5(14) fixes the insolvency resolution process period at 180 days beginning from the insolvency commencement date, that is, the date of admission of the application, and ending on the one hundred and eightieth day. The initiation date under Section 5(11) is the date the application is made, not the date it is admitted, so a period measured from it would be wrong.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: Vaigai Components Limited owes a supplier an amount under an invoice which fell due on 1 April and of which one instalment remains unpaid. Which statement correctly applies Sections 3(6), 3(11) and 3(12)?

options.A: There is a claim only, since a debt arises under the Code only after the liability has been decreed by a court
options.B: There is a debt and a default, but no claim, since a claim arises only on the public announcement of the process
options.C: There is a claim, a debt and a default, since non-payment of even part of the amount due amounts to default
options.D: There is a claim and a debt, but no default, because default arises only when the whole of the debt has fallen due

answer_html:
Answer: (C) There is a claim, a debt and a default, since non-payment of even part of the amount due amounts to default.

A claim under Section 3(6) is a right to payment whether or not it is reduced to judgment, matured or disputed. A debt under Section 3(11) is a liability or obligation in respect of a claim which is due from any person. Default under Section 3(12) is non-payment of debt when the whole or any part or instalment of the amount has become due and payable and is not paid, so part payment does not save the debtor from default.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: Under Section 6, where a corporate debtor commits a default, the corporate insolvency resolution process in respect of it may be initiated by-

options.A: a financial creditor, an operational creditor or the corporate debtor itself
options.B: a financial creditor or the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India alone
options.C: any shareholder holding not less than ten per cent of the paid-up capital
options.D: the Central Government on a reference made to it by the corporate debtor

answer_html:
Answer: (A) a financial creditor, an operational creditor or the corporate debtor itself.

Section 6 permits a financial creditor, an operational creditor or the corporate debtor itself to initiate the process on the occurrence of a default. Section 11 then bars a corporate debtor which is already undergoing the process, which completed a process in the preceding twelve months, which has violated the terms of a resolution plan approved in the preceding twelve months, or in respect of which a liquidation order has been made.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: Which of the following is prohibited by the moratorium declared under Section 14(1)?

options.A: The supply of essential goods or services to the corporate debtor by its existing suppliers
options.B: The enforcement of a guarantee against a surety in a contract of guarantee to the corporate debtor
options.C: The management of the operations of the corporate debtor as a going concern by the professional
options.D: The institution of a suit against the corporate debtor, and the execution of a decree already obtained

answer_html:
Answer: (D) The institution of a suit against the corporate debtor, and the execution of a decree already obtained.

Section 14(1) prohibits the institution or continuation of suits and proceedings against the corporate debtor including the execution of any judgment or decree, the transfer or disposal of its assets, any action to enforce a security interest including action under the SARFAESI Act, 2002, and the recovery of property by an owner or lessor. The supply of essential goods or services may not be terminated during the moratorium, and Section 14(3) puts a surety in a contract of guarantee outside the moratorium.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: An operational creditor has delivered a demand notice under Section 8 together with a copy of the invoice. It becomes entitled to apply to the Adjudicating Authority if the corporate debtor does not reply within-

options.A: fourteen days of the delivery of the demand notice or copy of the invoice
options.B: thirty days of the delivery of the demand notice or copy of the invoice
options.C: ten days of the delivery of the demand notice or copy of the invoice
options.D: seven days of the delivery of the demand notice or copy of the invoice

answer_html:
Answer: (C) ten days of the delivery of the demand notice or copy of the invoice.

Under Section 8(2) the corporate debtor must, within ten days of receipt of the demand notice or copy of the invoice, either bring to the notice of the operational creditor the existence of a dispute or record of a pending suit or arbitration, or furnish proof of payment. If no reply is received within those ten days the operational creditor may file an application under Section 9. The period of fourteen days is the time allowed to the Adjudicating Authority to admit or reject the application, and seven days is the time allowed to rectify defects.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: In reply to a demand notice the corporate debtor gives notice of a dispute and produces the record of a pending arbitration relating to the quality of the goods supplied. The Adjudicating Authority-

options.A: shall admit the application if it is satisfied on the merits that the dispute raised is not a bona fide one
options.B: shall refer the dispute to the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India for its opinion before proceeding
options.C: shall admit the application, since a pending arbitration is not a dispute within Section 5(6) of the Code
options.D: shall not admit the application, and is not required to examine whether the dispute is genuine or bogus

answer_html:
Answer: (D) shall not admit the application, and is not required to examine whether the dispute is genuine or bogus.

Dispute under Section 5(6) includes a suit or arbitration proceeding relating to the existence of the amount of the debt, the quality of goods or services, or the breach of a representation or warranty. Where a notice of dispute has been received the application under Section 9 will not be admitted at all, and the Adjudicating Authority is not empowered to go into the question whether the dispute is genuine or bogus.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: Which of the following persons is eligible to submit a resolution plan notwithstanding Section 29A?

options.A: A person who has executed a guarantee in favour of a creditor in respect of the corporate debtor, the guarantee having since been invoked
options.B: A person whose account was classified as a non-performing asset but who has paid all overdue amounts with interest and charges before submitting the plan
options.C: A person who is an undischarged insolvent, notwithstanding that his insolvency arose out of a business wholly unconnected with the corporate debtor
options.D: A person disqualified to act as a director under the Companies Act, 2013, notwithstanding that the disqualification is capable of being removed

answer_html:
Answer: (B) A person whose account was classified as a non-performing asset but who has paid all overdue amounts with interest and charges before submitting the plan.

The proviso to clause (c) of Section 29A allows a person whose account, or the account of a corporate debtor under his management or control, has been classified as a non-performing asset to submit a resolution plan if he makes payment of all overdue amounts with interest and charges relating to the non-performing asset account before submission of the plan. The disabilities in clauses (a), (e) and (h) are not curable in that manner.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: The resolution professional proposes to raise interim finance and to create a security interest over the assets of the corporate debtor. He may do so-

options.A: only with the prior approval of the committee of creditors by a vote of 66% of the voting shares
options.B: only with the prior approval of the Adjudicating Authority on an application made for the purpose
options.C: without any approval, since raising interim finance is incidental to running the debtor as a going concern
options.D: only with the prior approval of the committee of creditors by a vote of 51% of the voting shares

answer_html:
Answer: (A) only with the prior approval of the committee of creditors by a vote of 66% of the voting shares.

Section 28 lists the actions which the resolution professional may take only with the prior approval of the committee of creditors by a vote of 66% of the voting shares. Raising interim finance and creating a security interest over the assets of the corporate debtor are the first two of them. An action taken without that approval is void and action may be taken against the professional.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: A resolution plan provides for payment to the operational creditors of an amount smaller than they would receive on a distribution under Section 53. The committee of creditors approves the plan with 80% of the voting share. The Adjudicating Authority-

options.A: shall approve the plan, since the majority obtained comfortably exceeds the 66% required by the Code
options.B: shall itself modify the plan so as to raise the amount payable to the operational creditors to that level
options.C: shall not approve the plan, since it fails the requirement of Section 30(2) as to operational creditors
options.D: shall approve the plan, since the commercial wisdom of the committee of creditors is not open to review

answer_html:
Answer: (C) shall not approve the plan, since it fails the requirement of Section 30(2) as to operational creditors.

Section 30(2)(b) requires a resolution plan to provide for payment of the debts of operational creditors of an amount not less than what they would have received in a liquidation of the corporate debtor under Section 53, or the amount they would have received had the plan proceeds been distributed in the order of priority in Section 53(1). The resolution professional may place before the committee only plans which conform to Section 30(2), and the Adjudicating Authority approves a plan under Section 31 only if it meets the requirements of the Code.
topic_text: Treatment of operational creditors in a resolution plan

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
case_facts_html:
On an application made by Girija Bank Limited, the National Company Law Tribunal admitted an application for the corporate insolvency resolution process of Vindhya Ferro Alloys Limited and appointed an interim resolution professional by the same order.

On collation of the claims received, the interim resolution professional determined the financial debt of the corporate debtor as follows: Girija Bank Limited ₹120 crore; Pushkar Bank Limited ₹60 crore; Sarayu Finance Limited, a non-banking financial company, ₹40 crore; and Hansa Holdings Private Limited ₹80 crore. Hansa Holdings Private Limited is a related party of the corporate debtor within the meaning of Section 5(24).

The operational debt of the corporate debtor aggregates ₹50 crore and is owed to a large number of trade suppliers. The total debt of the corporate debtor is accordingly ₹350 crore.
question_html: Refer to the case scenario. The voting share of Girija Bank Limited in the committee of creditors of Vindhya Ferro Alloys Limited is-

options.A: 34.29 per cent
options.B: 66.67 per cent
options.C: 54.55 per cent
options.D: 40.00 per cent

answer_html:
Answer: (C) 54.55 per cent.

A related party to whom the corporate debtor owes a financial debt has no right of representation, participation or voting in the committee, so the ₹80 crore owed to Hansa Holdings Private Limited is left out. The voting share is the proportion of the financial debt owed to a financial creditor to the total financial debt reckoned for the committee, that is ₹120 crore out of ₹220 crore, which is 54.55 per cent. Working on ₹300 crore of financial debt gives 40.00 per cent, working on the total debt of ₹350 crore gives 34.29 per cent, and leaving out the non-banking financial company gives 66.67 per cent.
topic_text: Voting share in the committee of creditors

Hansa Holdings Private Limited is a related party of the corporate debtor within the meaning of Section 5(24).

The operational debt of the corporate debtor aggregates ₹50 crore and is owed to a large number of trade suppliers. The total debt of the corporate debtor is accordingly ₹350 crore.
question_html: Refer to the case scenario. Girija Bank Limited and Sarayu Finance Limited vote in favour of instructing the resolution professional to apply for an extension of the process beyond 180 days; Pushkar Bank Limited votes against. The position is that-

options.A: the instruction is valid, and the Adjudicating Authority is bound to grant the full extension once the committee of creditors has so resolved
options.B: the instruction is valid, and the Adjudicating Authority may extend the process by such further period as it thinks fit, not exceeding 90 days
options.C: the instruction is invalid, because an instruction to seek an extension requires a vote of 75% of the voting share of the financial creditors
options.D: the instruction is invalid, because an extension may be sought only where every financial creditor on the committee votes in favour of it

answer_html:
Answer: (B) the instruction is valid, and the Adjudicating Authority may extend the process by such further period as it thinks fit, not exceeding 90 days.

The two creditors voting in favour hold ₹160 crore of the ₹220 crore of financial debt reckoned for the committee, a voting share of 72.73 per cent, which satisfies the requirement of a vote of 66% of the voting shares under Section 12(2). On such an instruction the resolution professional applies to the Adjudicating Authority, which may extend the duration by such further period as it thinks fit but not exceeding 90 days. The extension is discretionary and is not granted as of right.

case_facts_html:
On an application made by Girija Bank Limited, the National Company Law Tribunal admitted an application for the corporate insolvency resolution process of Vindhya Ferro Alloys Limited and appointed an interim resolution professional by the same order.

On collation of the claims received, the interim resolution professional determined the financial debt of the corporate debtor as follows: Girija Bank Limited ₹120 crore; Pushkar Bank Limited ₹60 crore; Sarayu Finance Limited, a non-banking financial company, ₹40 crore; and Hansa Holdings Private Limited ₹80 crore. Hansa Holdings Private Limited is a related party of the corporate debtor within the meaning of Section 5(24).

The operational debt of the corporate debtor aggregates ₹50 crore and is owed to a large number of trade suppliers. The total debt of the corporate debtor is accordingly ₹350 crore.
question_html: Refer to the case scenario. Which statement about attendance at the meetings of the committee of creditors of Vindhya Ferro Alloys Limited is correct?

options.A: Hansa Holdings has no right of representation, participation or voting, while a representative of the operational creditors may attend without any right to vote
options.B: Hansa Holdings may participate and vote to the extent of the financial debt owed to it, while the operational creditors have no right to attend the meetings at all
options.C: Hansa Holdings may participate but not vote, while the operational creditors may attend and vote to the extent of the operational debt owed to them
options.D: Both Hansa Holdings and a representative of the operational creditors may attend and vote, each of them holding more than one-tenth of the total debt

answer_html:
Answer: (A) Hansa Holdings has no right of representation, participation or voting, while a representative of the operational creditors may attend without any right to vote.

A related party to whom the corporate debtor owes a financial debt has no right of representation, participation or voting in a meeting of the committee of creditors. Under Section 24 notice of the meeting goes to the members of the committee, to the members of the suspended Board of Directors, and to the operational creditors or their representative where their aggregate dues are not less than ten per cent of the debt. Here the operational dues of ₹50 crore are more than one-tenth of the total debt of ₹350 crore, so a representative may attend, but directors, partners and that representative have no right to vote.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: The Adjudicating Authority shall pass an order requiring the corporate debtor to be liquidated where-

options.A: the corporate debtor fails to pay the insolvency resolution process costs within thirty days of demand
options.B: the interim resolution professional is unable to constitute the committee of creditors within seven days
options.C: the audited accounts of the corporate debtor disclose liabilities exceeding the value of its assets
options.D: it does not receive a resolution plan before the expiry of the maximum period permitted for the process

answer_html:
Answer: (D) it does not receive a resolution plan before the expiry of the maximum period permitted for the process.

Under Section 33 a liquidation order follows where the Adjudicating Authority does not receive a resolution plan before the expiry of the insolvency resolution process period or the maximum period permitted, or rejects the plan for non-compliance with the requirements of Section 31. A liquidation order also follows where the committee of creditors resolves with 66% of the voting share to liquidate the corporate debtor at any time before confirmation of a resolution plan, and where an approved plan is contravened by the corporate debtor.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: A secured creditor which elects to realise its security interest outside the liquidation estate recovers, on enforcement, an amount in excess of the debt due to it. It must-

options.A: account to the liquidator for the surplus after adjusting the actual costs of realisation, and tender those funds to him
options.B: retain the surplus, the security interest having been realised outside the liquidation estate under Section 52
options.C: distribute the surplus among the unsecured financial creditors in proportion to their admitted claims
options.D: deposit the surplus with the Adjudicating Authority, which will then decide the manner of its distribution

answer_html:
Answer: (A) account to the liquidator for the surplus after adjusting the actual costs of realisation, and tender those funds to him.

Section 52 gives a secured creditor in liquidation the choice of relinquishing its security interest to the liquidation estate and receiving proceeds in the manner specified in Section 53, or of realising the security interest itself. Where enforcement yields proceeds in excess of the debts due to the secured creditor, it must account to the liquidator for the surplus after adjusting the actual costs of realisation, and tender the surplus funds to the liquidator.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: For the purposes of avoidance of undervalued transactions under Sections 45 and 46, the relevant period is-

options.A: one year preceding the insolvency commencement date, and two years where the counterparty is a related party
options.B: two years preceding the insolvency commencement date, and three years where the counterparty is a related party
options.C: one year preceding the liquidation commencement date, and two years where the counterparty is a related party
options.D: six months preceding the insolvency commencement date, and one year where the counterparty is a related party

answer_html:
Answer: (A) one year preceding the insolvency commencement date, and two years where the counterparty is a related party.

Section 46 fixes the relevant period at one year preceding the insolvency commencement date, and at two years preceding that date where the transaction is with a related party. A transaction is undervalued where the corporate debtor makes a gift to a person, or enters into a transaction for a consideration significantly less than the market value. If the liquidator or resolution professional does not apply, a creditor, member or partner of the corporate debtor may apply to have the transaction declared void.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
case_facts_html:
The Adjudicating Authority has passed an order for the liquidation of Narmada Steel Tubes Limited, the liquidation commencement date being 1 April 2025. The liquidator has realised ₹100 crore from the sale of the assets forming part of the liquidation estate.

The claims admitted by the liquidator are as follows: insolvency resolution process costs and liquidation costs ₹6 crore; workmen's dues for the twenty-four months preceding the liquidation commencement date ₹14 crore; Chenab Bank Limited ₹50 crore, that bank having relinquished its security interest to the liquidation estate; wages and unpaid dues owed to employees other than workmen for the twelve months preceding the liquidation commencement date ₹10 crore; financial debts owed to unsecured creditors ₹40 crore; and dues of the Central Government in respect of the two years preceding the liquidation commencement date ₹8 crore.
question_html: Refer to the case scenario. Applying the order of priority in Section 53, the amount available for distribution to the unsecured financial creditors of Narmada Steel Tubes Limited is-

options.A: ₹12 crore
options.B: ₹20 crore
options.C: ₹30 crore
options.D: ₹26 crore

answer_html:
Answer: (B) ₹20 crore.

The process and liquidation costs of ₹6 crore are paid in full first, leaving ₹94 crore. Workmen's dues of ₹14 crore for the twenty-four months preceding the liquidation commencement date and the ₹50 crore owed to the bank which relinquished its security rank equally and absorb ₹64 crore, leaving ₹30 crore. Wages of employees other than workmen for the preceding twelve months take ₹10 crore, leaving ₹20 crore for the unsecured financial creditors. Omitting the wages of other employees gives ₹30 crore, ignoring the costs payable in priority gives ₹26 crore, and paying the Government dues first gives ₹12 crore.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
case_facts_html:
The Adjudicating Authority has passed an order for the liquidation of Narmada Steel Tubes Limited, the liquidation commencement date being 1 April 2025. The liquidator has realised ₹100 crore from the sale of the assets forming part of the liquidation estate.

The claims admitted by the liquidator are as follows: insolvency resolution process costs and liquidation costs ₹6 crore; workmen's dues for the twenty-four months preceding the liquidation commencement date ₹14 crore; Chenab Bank Limited ₹50 crore, that bank having relinquished its security interest to the liquidation estate; wages and unpaid dues owed to employees other than workmen for the twelve months preceding the liquidation commencement date ₹10 crore; financial debts owed to unsecured creditors ₹40 crore; and dues of the Central Government in respect of the two years preceding the liquidation commencement date ₹8 crore.
question_html: Refer to the case scenario. On the distribution of the ₹100 crore realised, the dues of the Central Government will receive-

options.A: ₹8 crore in full, Government dues ranking equally with the wages of employees other than workmen
options.B: ₹4 crore, Government dues ranking equally with the financial debts owed to the unsecured creditors
options.C: nothing, the proceeds being exhausted at the level of the financial debts owed to unsecured creditors
options.D: ₹8 crore in full, Government dues being payable in priority to all debts owed to unsecured creditors

answer_html:
Answer: (C) nothing, the proceeds being exhausted at the level of the financial debts owed to unsecured creditors.

Amounts due to the Central and State Governments in respect of the two years preceding the liquidation commencement date rank in clause (e) of Section 53(1), below the financial debts owed to unsecured creditors in clause (d). The unsecured financial creditors have admitted claims of ₹40 crore against only ₹20 crore available, so the fund is exhausted before clause (e) is reached and the Government dues receive nothing. One of the stated objects of the Code is precisely this alteration in the order of priority of payment of Government dues.

question_html: Refer to the case scenario. If the liquidator had realised only ₹38 crore instead of ₹100 crore, the amount receivable by Chenab Bank Limited would be-

options.A: ₹25 crore, being its proportionate share of the ₹32 crore left after paying the costs in priority
options.B: ₹29.69 crore, being its proportionate share of the whole of the ₹38 crore realised by the liquidator
options.C: ₹32 crore, a secured creditor which has relinquished its security being paid before the workmen's dues
options.D: ₹19 crore, being one half of the realisation, the other half being reserved for the workmen's dues

answer_html:
Answer: (A) ₹25 crore, being its proportionate share of the ₹32 crore left after paying the costs in priority.

The costs of ₹6 crore are paid in full first, leaving ₹32 crore. The workmen's dues of ₹14 crore and the ₹50 crore owed to the bank which relinquished its security rank equally between and among themselves in clause (b) of Section 53(1), so the ₹32 crore is shared in the ratio of 14 to 50. The bank receives 50 divided by 64 of ₹32 crore, that is ₹25 crore, and the workmen receive ₹7 crore. Applying the ratio to the gross realisation without first paying the costs gives ₹29.69 crore.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: In relation to the insolvency and bankruptcy of individuals and partnership firms, the Adjudicating Authority is-

options.A: the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India, acting through the insolvency professional agency of which the trustee is a member
options.B: the Debt Recovery Tribunal having territorial jurisdiction over the place where the debtor resides or carries on business
options.C: the National Company Law Tribunal having territorial jurisdiction over the place where the debtor resides or works for gain
options.D: the civil court of ordinary original jurisdiction within whose local limits the individual debtor resides or works for gain

answer_html:
Answer: (B) the Debt Recovery Tribunal having territorial jurisdiction over the place where the debtor resides or carries on business.

Chapter VI of Part III provides that the Adjudicating Authority in relation to insolvency matters of individuals and firms is the Debt Recovery Tribunal having territorial jurisdiction over the place where the individual debtor actually and voluntarily resides or carries on business or personally works for gain. The Tribunal functions as a court under the Code of Civil Procedure, and the civil court has no jurisdiction in these matters.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: An order of the Debt Recovery Tribunal in a personal insolvency matter may be appealed against-

options.A: to the jurisdictional High Court within forty-five days, and thereafter to the Supreme Court on any question whatsoever
options.B: to the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal within ninety days, and thereafter to the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board
options.C: to the Debt Recovery Appellate Tribunal within fifteen days, and thereafter to the Supreme Court on a question of law
options.D: to the Debt Recovery Appellate Tribunal within thirty days, and thereafter to the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal

answer_html:
Answer: (C) to the Debt Recovery Appellate Tribunal within fifteen days, and thereafter to the Supreme Court on a question of law.

A decision of the Debt Recovery Tribunal may be appealed to the Debt Recovery Appellate Tribunal within fifteen days, and the decision of the Appellate Tribunal may be appealed to the Supreme Court on a question of law. The National Company Law Tribunal and the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal are the corresponding authorities for corporate persons, not for individuals and partnership firms.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: On the filing of an application for bankruptcy in respect of an individual, an interim moratorium-

options.A: commences only when the Adjudicating Authority admits the application and confirms the appointment of the bankruptcy trustee
options.B: commences on the date of the application but leaves the creditors free to institute fresh proceedings against the debtor
options.C: commences on the date of the order passed under Section 126 and continues until the bankrupt is discharged from his debts
options.D: commences on the date of the application and continues till the bankruptcy commencement date, staying all pending litigation

answer_html:
Answer: (D) commences on the date of the application and continues till the bankruptcy commencement date, staying all pending litigation.

The interim moratorium commences on the date of the application and operates on all the properties of the debtor until the commencement date. During the interim moratorium all pending legal proceedings are deemed to be stayed and no fresh legal action may be initiated, subject to any notification issued by the Central Government. The order under Section 126 is passed later, within fourteen days of confirmation of the trustee by the Board.
